newsitem.title: USA: US congressional panel issues draft of bank reform.
newsitem.headline: US congressional panel issues draft of bank reform.

text.p: Legislators working to overhaul antiquated U.S. banking laws issued a draft proposal late Tuesday for consideration by the House Banking Committee next week.
The proposal was issued to House Banking Committee members by committee chairman Jim Leach.

The draft, cobbled together from three earlier bills and a Clinton administration proposal, would eliminate most of the Depression era laws separating banking from other financial services such as insurance and securities underwriting.
But the draft included no language on whether banks should be allowed to venture farther afield and engage in commercial activities.

That question will be answered June 17, when the banking committee begins to debate the draft. Numerous amendments are expected on the banking and commerce issue, ranging from an outright ban on any mixing to allowing unfettered combinations of banks and nonfinancial companies.

Congress has been debating proposals to scrap the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act for more than a decade. But the initiatives have always broken down when the major financial industries were unable to reach a consensus.
In a cover memo attached to the draft, Leach, an Iowa Republican, acknowledged the difficult task ahead and warned that the proposal would not please all sides.

"In the context of so many differing perspectives of self interest within and between industry groups and in the context of differing views of the public interest, the goal is not to satisfy all parties but to be as fair as possible to each and as advancing as possible of the public interest," Leach wrote.
Leach said the discussion draft was not final and would likely be altered before the mark-up, or formal committee consideration, next week.

If the proposal became law, banks could affiliate with insurance companies and securities firms. Bank holding companies would be allowed to engage in new financial activities, which would include securities, insurance, merchant banking and any other activities that a newly created Council on Financial Services considered to be "financial taking into consideration changes in the marketplace and technology, such as providing encryption services," it said.

Banks would be allowed to have direct subsidiaries engaged in most nonbank financial activities. But merchant banking, insurance underwriting and real estate development activities would have to be done through holding company affiliates. Banks would be permitted to directly underwrite municipal revenue bonds.

The council would comprised the Secretaries of Treasury and Commerce, federal bank regulators, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and two state insurance representatives.
A similiar provision in the Clinton bank reform plan was strongly criticized by SEC chairman Arthur Levitt and the insurance industry as being too heavily weighted towards federal bank regulators.

The Fed would continue to regulate bank holding copmpanies, although "under a modified scheme that reduces regulatory burdens and takes into consideration the new affiliation rights provided," Leach's memo said.

Existing restrictions on loans and other transactions between nonbank affiliates and banks would continue to apply at the holding company level and would be extended to bank subsidiaries engaged in new financial activities, it said.

Savings and loan institutions, which once formed the core of the nation's mortgage lending market, would all but disappear as separate entities. The federal thrift charter and the Office of Thrift Supervision would be abolished. The more generous affiliation rights of diversified savings and loan holding companies would be grandfathered.

To resolve a dispute between banks and insurance companies over proper regulation of bank insurance sales, the draft would create a new self-regulating organization to provide uniform state licensing standards for insurance agents.

Any company could start a so-called wholesale financial institution. The bank-like entity's powers were somwhat circumscribed from earlier proposals. Wholesale banks would not carry federal deposit insurance and could not take deposits from retail customers or for less than $100,000. A company which owned a wholesale bank but no federally insured depository institutions would be allowed greater flexibility for non-financial, commercial investments.
